aiTitle: Add bench test for zero-copy IPC with tprobe2

content.text:
I'd try **iceoryx2** first.

Reasons:

- It's the purpose-built zero-copy IPC crate in Rust — shared-memory pub/sub where the payload is constructed directly in a shared-memory loan and the subscriber reads it in place. No serialization, no copies, which is exactly the property you want to measure.
- Pure Rust (unlike the original iceoryx C++ bindings), actively maintained, and its own benchmarks report sub-microsecond latencies, so it's in the range where TProbe2's rdtsc-level resolution actually matters.
- The API maps cleanly onto a bench loop: `loan_uninit` → write → `send` on one side, `receive` → read in place → drop on the other. Easy places to drop `tp.start()`/`tp.end()` probes.

Alternatives, in the order I'd consider them:

- **Hand-rolled `memmap2` + SPSC ring buffer** — not a crate solution, but the best *baseline*: it's the theoretical floor for shared-memory IPC, useful to see how much overhead iceoryx2 adds. Might be worth doing second as a comparison bench.
- **shared_memory crate** — just gives you a named shm region; you still build the ring yourself, so it's basically the baseline option with less control than memmap2.
- **rkyv over a socket/shm** — "zero-copy deserialization" but not zero-copy transport; different thing than what you're measuring.

One design note: iceoryx2 is cross-*process*, so a realistic bench needs two processes (or at minimum two threads with the intra-process backend), and TProbe2's records would be collected per-process. Worth deciding early whether the bench measures same-process ping-pong (simpler, thread-to-thread) or true cross-process round-trip.

Want me to sketch what the bench crate/binary layout would look like before touching anything?

content.text:
That combination — inter- **and** intra-process, zero-copy, `no_std` — is a niche no existing crate fills cleanly, as far as I know:

- **iceoryx2** — inter-process (and same-process works), but firmly `std`: it needs an OS for shm files, named concepts, etc. Their roadmap mentions bare-metal ambitions, but today it's not `no_std`.
- **bbqueue** — genuinely `no_std` (built for embedded/DMA), zero-copy grant-based SPSC ring. But its producer/consumer handles contain regular pointers into one address space, so it's intra-process only; you can't drop it into shared memory across processes as-is.
- **heapless::spsc**, **rtrb**, **ringbuf** — same story: good rings, but either not cross-process-safe (pointers, not offsets) or not `no_std` (rtrb).

The reason it's rare: cross-process safety requires the ring's state to be **offset-based and position-independent** (the region maps at different addresses in each process) and all coordination to go through atomics in the shared region. Most `no_std` rings assume a single address space; most shm crates assume `std`.

So the honest recommendation is a small hand-rolled core:

- A `no_std` SPSC ring crate of your own: header (atomic read/write indices) + payload area, all offset-addressed, operating on any `&mut [u8]`/raw region you give it. Zero-copy via grant-style APIs (write-in-place, read-in-place) like bbqueue's.
- Thin `std` adapters for the bench: intra-process = a `Box<[u8]>` shared between threads; inter-process = the same bytes in a `memfd`/`shm_open` region via `memmap2`.

That gives you one code path benched in both configurations with TProbe2, which is a nicer experiment anyway — same ring, only the memory substrate changes. And it's very much in this project's spirit (measuring the primitive itself rather than a framework).

If you'd rather start from an existing crate and adapt, **bbqueue** is the best donor — its grant API is the right shape; the work would be converting its handle state to offsets-in-region. But I'd guess writing a minimal SPSC ring from scratch is less work than retrofitting bbqueue.

Want me to check crates.io/GitHub for anything newer that fills this niche before we commit to hand-rolling? (My knowledge could be stale here.)

content.text:
`zerocopy` is complementary, not competing — it solves a different half of the problem.

What it is: Google's safe-transmutation crate. You derive `FromBytes` / `IntoBytes` / `KnownLayout` / `Immutable` on your message types, and it lets you reinterpret a `&[u8]` as `&YourType` (and back) with zero copying and no `unsafe`, with compile-time layout checks. It's fully `no_std` and has no dependencies to speak of.

What it is **not**: a transport. It has no ring buffer, no shared memory, no synchronization, no producer/consumer — it just makes "these bytes in place *are* my struct" safe.

So in the design from the last message, zerocopy slots in perfectly as the payload layer:

- The hand-rolled `no_std` SPSC ring moves raw byte grants through the region (intra- or inter-process).
- `zerocopy` types those bytes: producer writes via `IntoBytes`, consumer reads via `FromBytes::ref_from_bytes` directly on the grant slice — no serialization step, no copy, and the compiler enforces that the type is actually safe to view that way (no padding leaks, no invalid bit patterns, pointer-free).

That last point matters for the cross-process case specifically: `FromBytes` types are by construction valid for any bit pattern and can't contain references — which is exactly the "position-independent, offset-only" discipline the shared region needs. Using zerocopy on the payload makes that constraint compiler-checked instead of convention.

So the stack I'd suggest: **own `no_std` ring (transport) + zerocopy (typed in-place access) + memmap2 in the std bench harness (inter-process substrate)**, with TProbe2 instrumenting the ring operations. Everything below the harness stays `no_std`.

  min-p99 is 8,086 ns (same-CCD) vs 8,140 ns (cross-CCD)

- **The dev4 "21 % regression" was cross-invocation drift.**
  Two separate runs minutes apart, different thermal /
  frequency / background-load states — not an
  apples-to-apples probe comparison. Running both benches in
  one invocation is the only honest A/B and gives the
  numbers above.

A mechanism-level explanation (why scope API wins at steady
state, why the margin shrinks with pinning, what drives the
~50 ns cross-CCD adder) would need microarch measurements —
L1/L2 miss rates, atomic contention, DRAM bandwidth
saturation on the record buffer, Infinity Fabric latency
counters. The data above shows the *what*; the *why* is
speculative without those.

### Memory characterization

`TProbe2` keeps every sample as a 24-byte `Record` in an
unbounded `Vec` until `report()`. At the unpinned -d 60 rate,
that's ~400 MB for a single probe. Well inside a typical
workstation's RAM but far past L3 — which is fine as long as
the write pattern stays streaming (it does). Two mitigations
are listed as out-of-scope for 0.9.0 and remain so:

- Pre-reserved capacity (`Vec::with_capacity`) to eliminate
  doubling-realloc tail spikes.
- Bounded / ring-buffer policy for long-running or unbounded
  recording.

### When to use which probe

Data-driven guidance:

- `TProbe` — when memory footprint is the binding constraint.
  RAM use is bounded by the fixed HDR histogram size
  regardless of sample count, so very long or very high-rate
  recording doesn't grow.
- `TProbe2` — default choice for new measurement code. Ties
  or wins tp-pc on throughput in every 60-second regime
  measured (unpinned +25 %, same-CCD +3.5 %, cross-CCD tie),
  so no hot-path reason to prefer the direct-histogram path.
  Required when you need record-order information (TSC
  timeline), or expect per-site grouping / background drain /
  trace retention to matter later. Cost is the growing record
  buffer (24 bytes per sample, unbounded until `report()`).

## Plan: zero-copy IPC bench — zc-ring + zerocopy (0.10.0-dev1)

Sketch of a bench measuring zero-copy IPC with `TProbe2`,
working both intra-process (two threads) and inter-process
(two processes over shared memory), with the transport core
kept `no_std`.

### Stack

Survey conclusion: no existing crate covers inter+intra
process, zero-copy, `no_std` at once. `iceoryx2` is
inter-process but `std`; `bbqueue` is `no_std` zero-copy but
its handles hold pointers into one address space, so
intra-process only. The gap is filled by a small hand-rolled
ring:

- **`zc-ring`** (new crate, `no_std`): SPSC ring operating on
  a caller-provided raw byte region. All state
  offset-addressed (position-independent — the region may map
  at different addresses in each process); coordination via
  atomic read/write indices living in a header inside the
  region itself. Zero-copy via bbqueue-style grant API:
  producer gets a write grant (slice into the region), fills
  in place, commits; consumer gets a read grant, reads in
  place, releases.
- **`zerocopy`** (Google's safe-transmutation crate, `no_std`):
  types the payload bytes. Producer writes via `IntoBytes`,
  consumer reads via `FromBytes::ref_from_bytes` directly on
  the grant slice. `FromBytes` types are valid for any bit
  pattern and pointer-free, which compiler-enforces exactly
  the discipline shared memory needs.
- **`memmap2`** (`std`, bench harness only): the inter-process
  substrate — a `memfd_create` region mapped in parent and
  child.

### Crate layout

Convert the repo root to a two-member workspace:

```
Cargo.toml            # [workspace] members = ["iiac-perf", "zc-ring"]
zc-ring/
  Cargo.toml          # no_std, deps: none (core only)
  src/
    lib.rs            # #![no_std]; public Producer/Consumer/split API
    header.rs         # region header layout: atomic indices, capacity,
                      #   magic/version (all offsets, no pointers)
    grant.rs          # WriteGrant / ReadGrant (in-place slices)
  tests/              # std tests: loopback, wraparound, torn-write
iiac-perf/            # existing crate moves under here unchanged
  Cargo.toml          # + deps: zc-ring, zerocopy, memmap2
  src/
    benches/
      zcr_1p.rs       # intra-process: Box<[u8]> region, 2 threads,
                      #   TProbe2 on send/recv scopes
      zcr_2p.rs       # inter-process: memfd + memmap2, fork/exec child,
                      #   same ring code, same probes
      zcr_common.rs   # shared payload types (zerocopy derives) +
                      #   round-trip helpers for both benches
```

Notes on the sketch:

- Same ring code in both benches; only the memory substrate
  changes (heap vs shm). That isolates the substrate cost —
  the interesting comparison.
- `zcr-2p` needs a second process: the bench binary re-execs
  itself with a hidden subcommand (child inherits the memfd
  fd), keeping everything in one binary.
- Inter-process probe collection: each process runs its own
  `TProbe2` and reports separately (records are
  process-local); child writes its report to a pipe or the
  parent prints both.
- The bot thinks the moved `iiac-perf/` subdirectory is the
  main friction point of the workspace conversion (paths in
  notes, `cargo install --path`, jj file moves) — worth
  confirming appetite before starting.

Recommended approach: **multi-step** (`0.10.0-devN`) —
workspace conversion, new crate, and two benches are too
exploratory for one commit. Rough step split: dev1 plan
marker + workspace conversion; dev2 `zc-ring` core + tests;
dev3 `zcr-1p`; dev4 `zcr-2p`; release `0.10.0`.

content.content:
vc-x1 0.66.0-0

Dual-repo commit+push+finalize in one resumable command.

Collapses today's manual Commit-Push-Finalize Flow into a
single subcommand with two interactive approval gates and a
state machine with persistent progress so interruptions can
resume without re-doing completed stages.

Stages: preflight (fmt/clippy/test) → review (approve diff)
→ message ($EDITOR / --title+--body, approve text) →
commit-app → commit-claude (skipped if clean) → bookmark-both
→ push-app → finalize-claude. Failures in commit-app /
commit-claude / bookmark-both roll both repos back via
`jj op restore` to the snapshot recorded before commit-app.
After push-app succeeds the remote boundary is crossed and
recovery is forward-only.

Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip the review gate. Saved state carries title/body
across resumes so only the first invocation needs them.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in both repos (positional form of `--bookmark`).
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in both repos (flag form; see positional)

  -V, --version
          Print the `vc-x1 X.Y.Z` banner as the first line, then continue. With
          no subcommand, prints the banner and exits.
          
          Replaces clap's auto-version (which would exit after printing): the
          banner now rides along with normal subcommand execution rather than
          gating it, so scripts can capture the version *and* the command's
          output in one invocation.

      --restart
          Clear any saved state file and start from stage 1

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --from <STAGE>
          Explicit stage to jump to (advanced / debug use)

          Possible values:
          - preflight:       Run fmt / clippy / test / install / retest
          - review:          Present diff for the first approval gate
          - message:         Compose / edit the commit message; present for
            second gate
          - commit-app:      Commit the app repo
          - commit-claude:   Commit the `.claude` session repo (skipped if
            empty)
          - bookmark-both:   Advance both bookmarks to `@-`
          - push-app:        `jj git push --bookmark <b> -R .`
          - finalize-claude: `vc-x1 finalize --repo .claude --squash --push <b>
            ...`

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate

      --status
          Print where the saved state thinks we are and exit

      --recheck
          Re-run `preflight` even on resume (default: skip if last run
          succeeded)

      --no-finalize
          Stop before `finalize-claude` so it can be run manually

      --dry-run
          Print the exact commands for every stage without side effects

      --title <STR>
          Commit title (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

      --body <STR>
          Commit body (skip `$EDITOR` for the message stage)

  -y, --yes
          Auto-approve interactive prompts (review gate, message-edit
          confirmation). Required when `--title` / `--body` aren't both supplied
          in non-interactive contexts

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
